content: Phosphorous acid, chemically represented as H3PO3, is one of the oxoacids of phosphorus. Other notable oxoacids include phosphoric acid (H3PO4) and hypophosphorous acid (H3PO2). It is important to note that reduced phosphorus compounds are typically named with an ous suffix. Alternative names for phosphorous acid include orthophosphorous acid and dihydroxyphosphine oxide. Structurally, it is represented as HP(O)(OH)2, which is the product of the hydrolysis of its acid anhydride, P4O6. This relationship is analogous to the connection between phosphoric acid (H3PO4) and its anhydride, P4O10. Phosphorous acid exists in equilibrium between two tautomers: the predominant form, HP(O)(OH)2, and a minor tautomer, P(OH)3. The latter is also referred to as phosphorous acid (IUPAC name: phosphorous acid) and has the CAS number 10294-56-1. It is sometimes called phosphorus acid or orthophosphorous acid. The dihydroxy form, HP(O)(OH)2, is also known as phosphonic acid. Many reduced phosphorus acids exhibit complex equilibria involving hydrogen atom shifts between oxygen and phosphorus atoms. In its solid state, HP(O)(OH)2 adopts a tetrahedral geometry, with one shorter P=O bond measuring 148 pm and two longer P-O(H) bonds measuring 154 pm. Phosphorous acid can be synthesized through the hydrolysis of phosphorus trichloride (PCl3) with water or steam. Alternatively, potassium phosphite can serve as a precursor. In this method, aqueous potassium phosphite is treated with an excess of hydrochloric acid. The solution is then concentrated, and the pure acid is isolated through precipitation with alcohols. Phosphorous acid can undergo polymerization to form oligophosphorous acids, which are composed of a few condensed phosphorous acid molecules with the loss of water. The general formula for these oligomers is (HPO)nOn-1(OH)2, where n represents the number of units (e.g., 2, 3, 4, etc.). Polyphosphorous acids, on the other hand, can consist of dozens of such units linked together, with water being eliminated for each additional unit. For the phosphonic acid tautomer, the oligomerization process involves the condensation of P(OH)3 units, resulting in a different general formula: (HO)2POn-2P(OH)2. Both polyphosphonic and polyphosphorous acids share the same chemical formula for a given n value. For instance, triphosphosphonic acid and triphosphorous acid both have the formula H5P3O7 when n equals 3. Larger oligophosphorous acids may contain multiple hydroxyl groups, which can lead to the formation of cyclic structures known as cyclophosphorous acids. However, these cyclic compounds may sometimes be misnamed, as they can include carbon-based rings with phosphorous acid side chains. Branching can also occur in both oligophosphorous and polyphosphorous acids, resulting in ultraoligophosphorous or ultrapolyphosphorous acids. Phosphorous acid is classified as a diprotic acid because only two of its three hydrogen atoms are ionizable under aqueous conditions. The hydrogen atom directly bonded to the central phosphorus atom is not readily ionizable. This contrasts with phosphoric acid, where all three hydrogen atoms are acidic. The monodeprotonated form of phosphorous acid, HP(O)2(OH)−, is known as the phosphite ion. The IUPAC name for this species is phosphonic acid, although this term is more commonly used for substituted derivatives, such as organic groups bonded to phosphorus. For example, methylphosphonic acid, (CH3)PO(OH)2, can form methylphosphonate esters. Both phosphorous acid and its deprotonated forms are effective reducing agents, although their reactions are not particularly rapid. They are oxidized to phosphoric acid or its salts and can reduce noble metal cations to their metallic forms. Phosphorous acid has several practical applications. It can be thermally decomposed at approximately 180°C to produce phosphine gas (PH3), a flammable and toxic compound. This method is advantageous because phosphine is difficult to store, but its gaseous form can be easily separated from the non-volatile phosphoric acid byproduct. In agriculture, phosphorous acid is widely used as a phosphatic fertilizer. It is also employed in the preparation of phosphite salts, such as monopotassium phosphite and aluminum phosphonite. These salts, as well as aqueous solutions of pure phosphorous acid, are effective in controlling various microbial plant diseases. For example, they are used to treat infections caused by phytophthora and pythium pathogens, which belong to the oomycetes class (commonly known as water molds). These pathogens are responsible for diseases such as dieback, root rot, and downy mildew. Phosphorous acid-based products are marketed under various trade names, such as Yates Anti-Rot in Australia and Aliette (aluminum salts of phosphorous acid, generically known as Fosetyl-Al) in the United States. In addition to its agricultural uses, phosphorous acid serves as a chemical reagent. It acts as a reducing agent, although it is less vigorous than hypophosphorous acid in this role.
